title: If we confess (1 John 1:8–9)
hook: if we say we have no sin we deceive ourselves

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word of life that hands had handled. Your line was seen and touched. Did your hand find the reminder you kept close? Day six hundred fourteen.

A map app can get you almost anywhere, with one condition. It has to know where you actually are. If the little blue dot is wrong, if it thinks you're downtown when you're stuck on a country road, every direction it gives you will be wrong too, no matter how confident the voice sounds. It can't route you home from a place you're pretending to be. A few lines into his first letter, John says something very like this about the soul. And he says it to people who believed, the faithful, not to strangers.
screen: `THE BLUE DOT HAS TO BE RIGHT.` → `NO ROUTE FROM A PRETEND PLACE.` → `JOHN SAYS IT TO BELIEVERS.`

segments.voice: The Douay-Rheims: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." Notice the we. John doesn't point at outsiders. He includes himself, the one who touched the word of life. The danger isn't sin so much as pretending, putting the blue dot somewhere it isn't. Then the turn: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all iniquity." The Greek word for confess is homologeo, from two pieces: same, and say. To confess is to say the same thing. To agree with God about what actually happened. Not to grovel, not to perform, just to stop arguing with the truth. And then John picks two surprising words for God. Faithful, because God promised to forgive and keeps his promises. And just. You might expect justice to be the thing standing in the way of forgiveness. John puts it on forgiveness's side. A few verses later he explains: we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, who is the atonement for our sins. Catholics hear this passage in several places. At the start of almost every Mass, the people confess together that they have sinned, before they hear the word. And in the sacrament of Penance, a person names their sins to a priest and hears the words of absolution. The Catechism quotes these very verses when it says that to receive God's mercy, we have to admit our faults. Mercy can't reach a place you insist you aren't standing.
screen: `WE DECEIVE OURSELVES.` · `HOMOLOGEO: TO SAY THE SAME THING.` · `FAITHFUL AND JUST TO FORGIVE.` · `AT MASS AND IN CONFESSION.` · then, large: `IF WE CONFESS OUR SINS, HE IS FAITHFUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one sin honestly. Sit quietly and breathe. Look back over the past few days, not hunting, just looking. One thing will probably surface on its own: something you said, something you didn't do, a way you treated someone. When it comes, don't defend it and don't drown in it. Just say it to yourself plainly, in one sentence, the way it actually happened. Say the same thing as the truth. If you pray, you can tell it to God and rest in John's line: he is faithful and just, to forgive. If you don't, just let the plain naming be enough for now. The bell holds the time.
If we confess. First John one: to say the same thing as the truth, and find God faithful and just to forgive. Today's word.
Your line: he is faithful to forgive. Today, if the thing you named hurt someone, take one step toward making it right. Day six hundred fourteen.

screen: `DAY 614 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IN DEED AND IN TRUTH.`

howItsDone: Catholics confess their sins together in the penitential act near the start of Mass, and individually in the sacrament of Penance, where a person names their sins to a priest and receives absolution; the Church asks Catholics to confess serious sins at least once a year.

fork.setup: you did something wrong last week. nobody saw, and it's already fading. what does John say about telling yourself you have no sin?
options: it's fine if no one was hurt.
you deceive yourself, and the truth is not in you.
it only matters if it comes out.
fork.reveal: John's warning is about pretending, not just about the sin. and the turn comes right after: if we confess, he is faithful and just to forgive.

original.note: Greek: (if) we confess (1 John 1:9), from homos, same, and legō, to say.

trapdoor: what you thought: confession means feeling terrible about yourself.
what it means: to agree with God about what really happened, and find him faithful and just to forgive.
what a scholar hears: homologeo, 'to say the same thing'; and John calls God 'just' to forgive, setting justice on mercy's side because of Christ the advocate (1 John 2:1–2).

sources.quoted: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all iniquity.

notes: Homologeō from homos + legō ('say the same thing'): standard etymology. Confirm.
1 John 2:2: Douay-Rheims reads 'propitiation'; the script paraphrases with 'atonement'. Confirm the word choice.
CCC 1847 quotes 1 John 1:8–9 after 'To receive his mercy, we must admit our faults.' Paraphrased. Confirm.
Penitential act at the start of Mass ('almost every Mass': it can be replaced by the sprinkling rite or omitted in some combined rites). Confirm phrasing.
Annual confession of grave sins (CCC 1457). Confirm.
